children: Federal Reserve policy signals and U.S. payroll reports accounted for most of the rise in 10-year Treasury yields since August 2020, according to research published by VoxEU/CEPR.

The study, by Paul Beaudry, Paolo Cavallino, and Tim Willems, found that 90% of the observed increase in the 10-year yield occurred within three-day windows surrounding payroll reports or speeches by senior Fed officials, including the chair, vice chair, and Christopher Waller. Those windows accounted for just 24% of trading days.

The same periods were responsible for 81% of the rise in markets' expected average short-term interest rate over the following decade, according to the findings shared by Wall Street Journal reporter Nick Timiraos on X.

The findings suggested that the increase in long-term borrowing costs was largely associated with investors revising their expectations for future short-term rates, rather than becoming increasingly concerned about holding long-term debt.
The chart showed the 10-year Treasury yield
climbing from its pandemic-era lows to roughly 470 basis points in 2026. The five-year, five-year forward rate followed a broadly similar trajectory, reaching around 500 basis points.
Meanwhile, the average expected short-term rate over the following 10 years rose to ~350 basis points, remaining below the other two measures toward the end of the chart.

All three measures rose sharply beginning in 2022, although their trajectories subsequently diverged. The 10-year yield and five-year forward rate fluctuated at elevated levels through 2024 and 2025 before climbing again in 2026, while the expected average short-term rate remained comparatively subdued.

The research linked much of the post-Covid increase in long-term yields to market reactions surrounding Fed communications and employment data, underscoring the role of changing expectations for future monetary policy.

title: Fed signals drive most of post-Covid rise in Treasury yields, study finds
